newsitem.title: SPAIN: Foreign veterans visit Spain Civil War battle site.
newsitem.headline: Foreign veterans visit Spain Civil War battle site.

text.p: Idealistic veterans of the International Brigades in Spain's Civil War, many of them octogenarians and confined to wheelchairs, revisited on Tuesday the site of one of their fiercest battles against fascism.
More than 400 survivors from 30 countries returned to Spain this week to remember, and be remembered for fighting with the Republicans against General Francisco Franco in the 1936-1939 war.

"They never took the bridge," said Fred Clarke, a veteran from England gazing at the Bridge of Arganda outside Madrid where Spain inaugurated a monument to the brigades on Tuesday. "It was 'no pasaran'" he said, recalling the battle cry that united the Republicans "They shall not pass."
More than 40,000 volunteers, many recruited by communist parties and trade unions in Europe and North America with support from the Soviet Union, took up arms for democracy in the Civil War.
They battled Franco's forces backed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy in a conflict which became an ideological rehearsal for World War Two.

The story of these men and women, young and old, poets and miners was romanticised in books such as George Orwell's "Homage to Catalonia" and films like British director Ken Loach's "Land and Freedom".
A third of the volunteers fell in battle and some survivors were too old or ill to travel to Spain for the week-long commemoration on the 60th anniversary of the war.
"We came in solidarity with the Spanish people but we were also fighting to defend our own homes," said Bill Alexander from London, one of the leaders of the British battalion in the war.
"When we got home to London, we pledged we would continue the fight against fascism on a different front."
The Spanish Republic lost the war, leaving Franco to rule as a dictator until he died in 1975.
The Bridge of Arganda on the outskirts of Madrid connected the city to Valencia and was the site of one of the toughest battles the International Brigades fought, veterans said on Tuesday.

"I remember how I used to run up and down these mountains as a message boy," said Wally Togwell of England looking out at the hills surrounding the monument. "It brings up memories that we fought here. We were the first to fight against fascism."
Upon their arrival in Spain, some of the elderly veterans wept, overwhelmed with emotion that they were being honoured for a cause they thought had been forgotten.
"It's wonderful," said American Jim Benet when he arrived at Madrid airport late Monday night.

"At the time we were here, we had no idea that we would be remembered after 60 years. It's hard to talk about it. There were people saying 'welcome' to us and they didn't know very much English but they knew that much," he said.
Many of the former fighters arrived in wheelchairs. Some swigged back whiskey and burst into patriotic songs in the arrival hall of the airport.
"I'm glad I lived for the 60th anniversary. I get very emotional," said Irishman Peter Connolly. "They're the most beautiful people in the world," he said of Spaniards.
